clinicalPearls: A triad of long-standing untreated primary hypothyroidism, incomplete isosexual precocious puberty and delayed bone age.
Almost uniquely among causes of precocious puberty, skeletal maturation is delayed rather than advanced — a key discriminating feature.
In girls there is thelarche and vaginal bleeding with enlarged multicystic ovaries; in boys, testicular enlargement occurs without significant virilisation.
Driven by markedly elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone acting on the follicle-stimulating hormone receptor, the so-called specificity spillover.
Growth is slowed or arrested despite pubertal signs — this paradox should point directly to hypothyroidism.
Hyperprolactinaemia is frequent, driven by elevated thyrotrophin-releasing hormone, and thyrotroph hyperplasia may enlarge the pituitary and mimic an adenoma.
Autoimmune (Hashimoto) hypothyroidism is the usual underlying cause.
Fully reversible with thyroid hormone replacement, so unnecessary ovarian or pituitary surgery should be avoided.
reference.pathophysiology: Long-standing, severe, untreated primary hypothyroidism removes negative feedback on the hypothalamic–pituitary axis, generating markedly elevated thyrotrophin-releasing hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Because thyroid-stimulating hormone shares a common alpha subunit and structural homology with the gonadotrophins, very high concentrations weakly cross-activate the follicle-stimulating hormone receptor — the specificity spillover phenomenon — stimulating ovarian follicular development with multicystic ovaries, oestradiol secretion, thelarche and vaginal bleeding in girls, and Sertoli-cell-driven testicular enlargement without significant androgen-mediated virilisation in boys. Elevated thyrotrophin-releasing hormone concurrently drives prolactin secretion, causing hyperprolactinaemia, and thyrotroph hyperplasia may enlarge the pituitary and mimic an adenoma. Crucially, the accompanying hypothyroid suppression of the growth hormone–IGF-1 axis retards skeletal maturation, so bone age is delayed rather than advanced — the opposite of most other causes of precocious puberty — and every feature regresses with thyroid hormone replacement.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral precocious puberty from an ovarian or adrenal tumour
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (where virilisation is present)
Pituitary macroadenoma as a cause of hyperprolactinaemia and pituitary enlargement
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests showing markedly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with low free thyroxine
Pelvic ultrasound to assess multicystic ovaries and uterine maturation
Gonadotrophins with oestradiol or testosterone, and a gonadotrophin-releasing hormone stimulation test where central puberty is considered
Pituitary MRI when a mass is suspected, to avoid mistaking thyrotroph hyperplasia for an adenoma
redFlags: Vaginal bleeding in a young child, which always warrants prompt evaluation
Rapidly enlarging ovarian cysts with a risk of torsion
Pituitary enlargement accompanied by headache or visual disturbance
Features of profound hypothyroidism such as myxoedema or a pericardial effusion
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent because the syndrome is reversible with thyroid hormone replacement, and the pubertal features and ovarian cysts regress. Catch-up may be incomplete and final height can be compromised when hypothyroidism has been prolonged.
pitfalls: Misreading pituitary thyrotroph hyperplasia as an adenoma and undertaking unnecessary pituitary surgery.
Operating on multicystic ovaries mistaken for a neoplasm when they would regress with thyroid hormone.
Expecting advanced bone age as in other forms of precocity and being misled by the delayed skeletal maturation.
Overlooking the underlying hypothyroidism because the pubertal signs dominate the presentation.
management: Thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine as the definitive, curative treatment, reversing the pubertal and ovarian changes
Gradual initiation of levothyroxine with monitoring, given the risks associated with rapid correction of long-standing hypothyroidism
Avoidance of unnecessary ovarian cyst surgery, since the multicystic ovaries are expected to regress on treatment
Monitoring of thyroid function, growth, bone age and pubertal progress during replacement
Reassurance that hyperprolactinaemia and thyrotroph or pituitary enlargement resolve with adequate replacement, avoiding unnecessary pituitary surgery
Paediatric endocrinology follow-up with attention to catch-up growth and final height
Investigation and management of the underlying cause of hypothyroidism such as autoimmune thyroiditis
